"Peripatetic" describes a person, a lifestyle, a career, or a way of doing something that is constantly moving from place to place — especially as a regular, defining feature rather than an occasional occurrence. A peripatetic person is always on the go, never settling in one location for long, perpetually in transit.

The single most important nuance: it's not just about traveling a lot.

What separates "peripatetic" from simply saying someone "travels a lot" is that the movement is a structural, defining characteristic. It's built into the very nature of the person's life or work. A businessperson who flies to another city twice a year for a conference is not peripatetic. But a management consultant who lives out of hotel rooms and works in a different city every single week — that is peripatetic. The movement isn't incidental. It is the life.

Think of a rural doctor who has no clinic and instead drives from village to village every week to treat patients. Or a journalist who has covered stories on six continents and never spends more than a few weeks in the same place. Or a classical musician perpetually on an international concert tour. Or a teacher assigned to work across five different schools in a district, driving between them throughout the week. These are peripatetic lives and peripatetic careers. Movement is the constant.
What kinds of things can be described as peripatetic?

While it most often describes people, it can describe anything connected to the idea of habitual movement. A peripatetic career is one that takes someone across many cities or countries. A peripatetic childhood is one where a child constantly moved homes and schools — perhaps because of a parent in the military, or a family that relocated frequently. A peripatetic existence or lifestyle describes a life organized around movement. You can even describe a working arrangement as peripatetic — for instance, "the team worked in a peripatetic fashion, operating from different locations each month."
The tone and feel of the word

"Peripatetic" is a fairly sophisticated, literary word. Choosing it over simpler alternatives like "traveling" or "always on the move" signals a certain intellectual weight and precision. It is not a negative word — it is essentially neutral in feeling — but context shapes its connotation. In some contexts it sounds faintly romantic, suggesting freedom, breadth of experience, and an adventurous spirit. In others, it carries a subtle undertone of rootlessness — a life without a stable anchor. Neither reading is built into the word itself; it picks up its emotional color from the surrounding sentence.

"She had a peripatetic academic career, holding positions at universities in Paris, Chicago, and Singapore."

"Growing up in a diplomatic family gave him a peripatetic childhood — a new country every two years."

"The organization relied on a small team of peripatetic trainers who traveled to different offices to run workshops."

"After years of a peripatetic lifestyle, she finally settled in one city and bought a home."

"He was a peripatetic consultant whose clients were spread across the continent."

There is a second, more narrow use of "peripatetic" — capitalized as Peripatetic — that you will encounter specifically in academic philosophy. In this context, it refers to the philosophy of Aristotle and his school of thought. When scholars write about Peripatetic philosophy or the Peripatetic school, they mean Aristotle's ideas and the tradition that followed from them. This usage is restricted almost entirely to academic writing about ancient Greek philosophy. If you ever see "Peripatetic" with a capital P in a philosophy text, it means Aristotelian. In everyday, non-academic writing, you will virtually always encounter it in its general sense — constant movement — and in lowercase.
If you ever need to instantly recall the word: peripatetic = always moving from place to place as a defining feature of one's life or work, never staying put.
